page.title: SpringSaLaD Import and Export
page.introduction: The standalone SpringSaLaD program keeps a whole system - molecules, reactions, counters, geometry, times - in a single plain text file. VCell reads and writes that format, with the extension .ssld, so a model built in one can be opened in the other.
page.appearance:
The format is a plain text file divided into named sections, each introduced by a line of asterisks. The sections are, in order: time information, spatial information, the molecules and their sites, the files those molecules were built from, then the reactions - decay, transition, allosteric and binding - then the counters: molecule, state, bond, site property and cluster.
Two things about it are worth knowing before relying on a round trip:
The MOLECULE_FILES section names the PDB source file each molecule was built from, if any. VCell looks for those beside the .ssld file and then in a structure_files folder next to it. A missing one is not fatal - the molecule is imported without it, and a note is written to the log - but if a model was produced by the standalone program's "Add PDB from file", keep that folder with it.
The format describes a SpringSaLaD system, not a VCell BioModel. Anything VCell holds that SpringSaLaD has no place for - other applications over the same physiology, annotations, simulations - is not in the file and does not survive the round trip.
page.operations:
Importing. File > Open > Local... and pick the .ssld file; it is one of the formats the model chooser accepts, beside .vcml, .sbml and .bngl. VCell builds a BioModel from it: the molecules with their sites, states, radii, diffusion rates, colours and positions; the reactions, each already carrying its subtype; and a SpringSaLaD application with the geometry and times the file described.
Exporting. With the SpringSaLaD application selected, File > Export... and choose SpringSaLaD format (.ssld) from the format list. The export is of one application, not of the whole BioModel, because a .ssld file describes exactly one system.
What can stop an export. The exporter writes the solver's own input, so a model that could not be solved cannot be written either. In particular, an application with no reactions at all cannot be exported: with nothing to classify, the model is not recognised as a Langevin model and the writer stops. Add at least one reaction rule before exporting a model you are still building.
When to use it. Import is the quickest way to bring an existing SpringSaLaD model into VCell, and it is a good deal quicker than rebuilding the site geometry by hand. Export is useful for taking a model to the standalone program, and for looking at exactly what the solver will be given - the file is readable, and every number in it came from somewhere in the application.
